youtube.baslik: Clinical Placement Prep: Your Day-One Checklist | Lesson 271 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
A checklist to prepare for the first day of an audiology clinical placement: professional behavior and patient communication, identity checks and instructions, the daily listening check and test room setup, hygiene, documentation and the privacy of personal health data. We also cover common student mistakes and the end-of-day review.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology; ASHA, Code of Ethics; Law No. 6698 on the Protection of Personal Data, Türkiye; WHO, Guidelines on Hand Hygiene in Health Care.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
With this lesson we begin the section on clinical preparation and adult cases.
We will look at how to prepare for the first day of placement under behavior, communication, pretest setup and documentation.
Clinical placement is the period when we turn coursework into practice with real patients in a real clinical setting.
There is a big difference between reading an audiogram in class and obtaining one step by step in the booth.
A student always works under a supervising audiologist; patient safety and accurate results are assured with that person's approval.
So on the first day you are expected to observe, ask and follow guidance rather than make decisions on your own.
Setting a few learning goals with your supervisor at the start of placement makes your progress visible.
For example, the first week might target otoscopy and daily checks, and later weeks doing masked bone conduction independently.

maddeler.metin: Learn the site's rules and hours

cumleler: Before day one, learn the site's working hours, dress code and the responsibilities expected of students.

cumleler.yazi: Clean, simple clothing, a visible ID badge and closed shoes matter for both patient safety and trust.
cumleler.ses: Clean, simple clothing, a visible I D badge and closed shoes matter for both patient safety and trust.

cumleler: Many sites ask for some health documents before placement, such as vaccination records; do not leave these to the last minute.
Keep a small notebook with you for short notes on abbreviations, masking rules and the clinic's protocols.
Briefly reviewing audiogram symbols, masking rules and tympanogram types the night before makes the first day much easier.
Professionalism is about attitude and behavior as well as knowledge; patients first know the clinic through your manner.
Being in the room before the appointment time, with equipment and forms ready, is what punctuality means.
When you meet the patient, say your name and that you are an audiology student on placement.
Your personal phone should be silent and out of sight near patients; distraction is a common cause of test errors.
Explaining results and their possible meaning to the patient is not your job unless your supervisor allows it.
When unsure of an answer, saying we will look at this together is always better than guessing.
Call the patient by name from the waiting area, introduce yourself and walk to the test room together.
For patient safety, identity is verified with two separate details, such as full name and date of birth, and checked against the file.
Then briefly explain which tests will be done and about how long they will take.
The patient's questions are answered and verbal consent to continue with testing is obtained.
Instructions are short and clear; one sentence like press the button when you hear even a very soft tone beats a long explanation.
You can check the instructions were understood by having the patient repeat in their own words what to do.

sahneler.baslik: *Communicating* with a person with hearing loss

maddeler.metin: Face them, light on your face
Talk to the patient, not companion

cumleler: Face the patient when you speak; the light should be on your face, not behind you, which makes speechreading easier.
Speak slowly and clearly but do not shout; shouting distorts the sound and can feel unpleasant.
When taking the history, close the door and choose a spot away from ventilation or computer noise.
After giving important information, ask the patient to summarize it in their own words; this is called the teach-back method.
Even if the patient comes with a family member, direct questions to the patient first; the companion adds information when needed.
The day starts by switching on the equipment; many devices need a short warm-up time to run stably.
Next comes the daily listening check of the audiometer; earphones, bone vibrator and loudspeaker are checked with your own ears.
Crackling in cables, crosstalk between channels and a working patient button are also part of this check.
The immittance volume reading is checked with the maker's test cavity; the otoacoustic emission probe is checked by clinic protocol.
Each check is logged with date and signature; if there is a problem, the device is not used that day and the person in charge is told.
We saw the details in the daily listening check lesson; on placement you will run this list every morning.
In the test room, first check the overall setup: does the door close fully, and do ventilation or air conditioning make noise?
The patient chair is placed so you can see the patient through the window, but the patient cannot see the audiometer panel.
Earphones, insert tips and the bone vibrator should be in place and clean.
The response button should be within the patient's reach, and the intercom should be tried before testing begins.
Unneeded items are removed from the booth; the patient's phone is switched off, and glasses and jewelry are removed if needed.
These small details directly affect the accuracy of thresholds and how smoothly the test runs.
Hand hygiene is done before and after every patient; it is the simplest but most effective infection measure in the clinic.
Earphone cushions, the bone vibrator and the response button are wiped with a site-approved product after every patient.
Parts such as insert foam tips are single use; probe tips are also replaced or cleaned according to protocol.
If otoscopy shows discharge, a wound or a foreign body in the ear canal, consult your supervisor before testing.
We will cover the details of infection control separately in a later lesson.

sahneler.metin: Start testing with otoscopy; never place earphones without seeing the ear canal.
cumleler: A tip from the field: start every test with otoscopy, and never place earphones without seeing the ear canal.
Impacted earwax, discharge or a collapsing ear canal can mislead even the most careful measurement.
Record what you see on otoscopy right away in a short note; it will help a lot when you write the report.
Show your supervisor any appearance you are unsure of; looking together is the fastest way to learn.
Documentation means writing down every procedure so it can be read and verified later.
The date, time, the student and supervisor, the type of earphone used and the masking levels must always be recorded.
How consistent the patient's responses were, in other words test reliability, is also an important part of the record.
Unexpected events, such as the patient stopping the test or describing dizziness, are added in a short note.
The record is completed the same day, while your memory is fresh, and submitted for your supervisor's approval.
A procedure that was not written down counts as not done for anyone who looks later.

ogeler.metin: Health data is a special category

cumleler.yazi: In Türkiye, the Personal Data Protection Law No. 6698, known as KVKK, treats health data as a special category of personal data.
cumleler.ses: In Türkiye, the Personal Data Protection Law No. sixty six ninety eight, known as KVKK, treats health data as a special category of personal data.

cumleler: So an audiogram or report is information that must be carefully protected.
Patients' names and findings are not discussed in hallways, elevators or the cafeteria.
No photos of the patient file, screen or audiogram are taken with a personal phone or shared on social media.
The screen is locked when you leave the computer; an open session can let someone else access the data.
In case presentations after placement, identifying details are removed, in other words the data are de-identified.

ogeler.metin: Saying this could be a tumor
Apply the rule for each ear

cumleler: A common mistake is presenting a finding to the patient as a diagnosis; a sentence like this could be a tumor is both wrong and harmful.
Skipping a masking rule under time pressure can invalidate the whole audiogram; apply the rules for each ear and each frequency.
Leaving records until the end of the day or the next day leads to forgotten details.
Not asking when unsure is also common; placement is the time when asking is most welcome.
At the end of the day, used parts are cleaned, equipment is switched off per site rules and the room is left ready for the next day.
Check that all records are complete and approved by the supervisor.
A short review with your supervisor shows what you did well and what you need to improve.
Write what you learned that day in a learning journal, without any identifying details.
Set a small goal for the next day; for example, tomorrow I will do bone conduction masking while my supervisor watches.
Clinical placement is when we turn coursework into clinical skill under a supervising audiologist.
In the first minutes with a patient, you introduce yourself, verify identity with two details and give short, clear instructions.
The day starts with the equipment listening check and test room setup; every test starts with otoscopy.
Records are completed the same day and kept confidential as health data.

sahneler.soru: What if a patient asks what the audiogram means?
secenekler: We explain it with the supervisor
sahneler.aciklama: Results are explained _with the supervisor's approval_; students do not diagnose.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: in your first week of placement, a patient asks you what their audiogram means. What is the best approach?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: explaining the result together with your supervisor.
Students do not diagnose or interpret alone; saying we will look at this together is both honest and reassuring.
